source: Langhout and Aniche (2021) Atoms of Confusion in Java (ICPC)
finding: Replication of Gopstein et al. (C, 2017) in Java. Small code patterns make novices misread what code does. With all atoms pooled, wrong answers were much more likely when an atom was present.
numbers: 132 CS students started, 96 finished (60% first-years). 80 snippets, 14 atoms. Pooled odds ratio 3.82, 95% CI 2.69 to 5.42.
limits: Novices only. Short snippets. Task was to predict the output. Snippet set was inherited from the C study and is subjective.
agent_relevance: A slip in reading code is real and predictable by pattern. A model reading code can slip the same way; check claims about code behaviour by running it (G2).

source: Langhout and Aniche (2021) Atoms of Confusion in Java (ICPC)
finding: Only some atoms replicate. 7 of 14 atoms gave significantly more errors. Others did not, and one atom went the wrong way.
numbers: Odds ratios 2.7 up to 56 for the 7 significant atoms. Participants rated the atom version as harder to read in 10 of 14. Repurposed variables: 12 wrong of 25 with the atom versus 18 wrong of 32 without. Infix operator precedence and indentation atoms: not significant. Seven C atoms had no Java form.
limits: Perceived confusion and actual error disagree for some atoms. Effects differ by language, so a breakdown list from one language does not transfer whole.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a fixed list of error-prone patterns. Measure which patterns break the agent, per language and per model.

source: Langhout and Aniche (2021) Atoms of Confusion in Java (ICPC)
finding: Authors say it is unknown whether experts are affected. They recommend avoiding the significant atoms or training all levels.
numbers: Open questions listed: experienced developers, larger snippets, Java-specific atoms, why language changes the result.
limits: No expert sample, so the slip-to-defect chain for experts is untested here.
agent_relevance: The expertise moderator is unmeasured in humans; for the agent, test per model size instead of assuming.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study (IEEE TSE)
finding: Systematic map of bias research in software engineering. Many studies, but thin theory and almost no mitigation evidence.
numbers: 65 articles (1990 to 2016), 37 biases, 47 empirical. Antecedents studied for only 11 biases, effects for 11. Debiasing covered 6 of 37 biases.
limits: Search stopped at 2016. A mapping, not a pooled effect size.
agent_relevance: The human evidence for bias-to-defect chains is weaker than the claims built on it. Treat bias checklists as unproven (consistent with section 4b).

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study (IEEE TSE)
finding: No replications, families of experiments or meta-analyses existed for cognitive bias in software engineering. Most studies cite no earlier work on the same bias.
numbers: Review reports zero replications, families of experiments or meta-analyses among 65 studies.
quote: we found no replications, families of experiments or meta-analyses
limits: Absence in 2016 may have changed; atoms of confusion got a replication in 2021.
agent_relevance: Nothing here is established by replication except the few later ones. Rate each human finding as single-study unless shown otherwise.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study (IEEE TSE)
finding: Debiasing proposals were all untested suggestions. Awareness alone does not remove bias. Changing the task is easier than changing the person.
numbers: Section 4.4: none of the primary studies gave strong empirical evidence for any debiasing technique. One idea: ask testers to seek evidence of failure.
limits: Authors still say simple interventions can work; that is opinion in the review, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and section 4b: be-careful prompts are not evidence-backed; change the task structure (run a test) instead.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study (IEEE TSE)
finding: Fixation had very thin direct evidence. One experiment: labelling desiderata as requirements made designers fixate more than labelling them ideas.
numbers: Only 1 primary study on fixation antecedents and effects (Mohanani, Ralph, Shreeve 2014).
limits: One study; a design task, not debugging.
agent_relevance: The wording of the task text can cause fixation; keep problem statements neutral when handing an agent a failed attempt.

source: Wyrich, Merz, Graziotin (2022) Anchoring Code Understandability Evaluations Through Task Descriptions (ICPC)
finding: A short description of a code snippet given before the task shifted people's rating of how understandable the code was. An earlier related study (Wyrich et al.) found a large effect with a fake metric score shown next to the code.
numbers: N=256 (206 students, 50 professionals). Path coefficient from scenario to perceived comprehensibility 0.165, p<.001. Model R2 = .223. Earlier study: effect size -1.29 for a shown value of 4 versus 8.
limits: Authors call it a conceptual, not exact, replication: the anchor was weaker and came earlier. Outcome is self-rated comprehension, not defect rate.
agent_relevance: A stated expectation in the prompt biases judgement of code. Hide authorship, scores and expected answers from a judge (G5).

source: Wyrich, Merz, Graziotin (2022) Anchoring Code Understandability Evaluations Through Task Descriptions (ICPC)
finding: Expertise did not protect. Professionals were anchored about as much as students. Snippet difficulty did not change the anchoring effect either.
numbers: Role to rating path and Scenario x Role interaction not significant. Difficulty x Scenario: 0.076, p>.10. Difficulty main effect 0.418, p<.001.
limits: Professionals were 50 of 256 and not a random sample; subgroup power is low.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a stronger model being immune; test anchoring per model.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Framing effect in code models. Adding irrelevant lines before a task makes Codex and CodeGen copy those lines and lose accuracy.
numbers: Codex accuracy fell 22.3 to 30.5 points across framing lines. The framing line was copied in 81% of Codex outputs and 70.7% of CodeGen outputs, versus 4.5% and 0.0% on unchanged prompts.
limits: Codex-era models (2021 to 2022), HumanEval-style functions. Not tested on current models.
agent_relevance: Any earlier buggy code left in context pulls the next attempt toward it. Strip failed code from the prompt unless it is needed as the failing output (G2).

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Anchoring in code models. A prepended function that is close to correct but wrong lowers accuracy, and its lines show up in the answer.
numbers: Print-var and add-var anchor functions lowered accuracy at every tested number of prompted solution lines (read from figures; no table values). Renaming the anchor function changed results only negligibly.
limits: Effect sizes are in plots; the text gives no single headline figure.
agent_relevance: A prior wrong attempt in context is a measurable defect source.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: The model follows a simple but wrong cue (the function name) against the spec, and does the first operation in a list before the right one.
numbers: Conflicting function name: Codex accuracy fell from 100% to 4.4 to 4.6%. Order flip: accuracy 50% to 17%; 75% of the flipped errors were unary-first outputs.
limits: Hand-built prompts; contrived conflicts.
agent_relevance: Names and surface cues can override instructions. Verify behaviour by running, not by reading names.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: A high-impact slip: Codex deleted files when more than a few packages were imported.
numbers: Wrong file deletion on at least 80% of prompts with 3 or more package imports, versus correct output on 90% of prompts with 2 or fewer.
limits: Single scenario, Codex only.
agent_relevance: Slips grow with task load, and some have costly effects. Gate destructive actions in code.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: GPT-3 davinci-001 shows human-like anchoring in estimate questions, a small replication of Jacowitz and Kahneman (1995).
numbers: 14 of 15 original questions, anchors at plus or minus 20% and 50% of the truth. When the estimate moved it equalled the anchor 67% of the time. About 41% of outputs were gibberish.
limits: Small sample, templates, old model, high gibberish rate.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence on its own. Use it only as a pointer.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri et al. (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development
finding: Partial replication of Chattopadhyay et al. (ICSE 2020) bias rates, with LLM use added. The bias share matched; the reversal rate did not.
numbers: 14 developers, 2,013 actions, 808 with an LLM. Actions linked to a bias: 47.14% versus 45.72% of 2,084 in the earlier study. Reversal 25% (505/2013) versus 52.9% (1104/2084) earlier.
limits: Small N, observation sessions, coders' judgement of biases. The reversal share halved, so the earlier headline did not carry over cleanly.
agent_relevance: The rate of bias is stable across studies; the harm per bias is not. Do not budget around a fixed harm figure.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri et al. (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development
finding: Actions using an LLM were more often biased and more often reversed. The old bias categories did not predict reversals well.
numbers: LLM actions: 53.7% biased, 29.4% reversed (chi-square, Bonferroni). Broader 15-category scheme: 56.4% of 808 LLM actions biased; 29.5% (238/808) reversed. Old categories: weak link to reversals.
limits: Observation of 14 people; no matched control group without an LLM.
agent_relevance: Accepting model output without checks is the dominant slip. Supports G2 and G3 for the agent's own accepted outputs.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri et al. (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development
finding: Fixation had the highest reversal rate among LLM-related biases: developers kept pasting the same fix after an error.
numbers: Fixation: 76 LLM actions, 33 reversed (43.4%), 7 participants. Instant gratification 156 actions, 46 reversed (29.5%). Suggester preference 102, 22 reversed (21.5%). Memory bias 80, 26 reversed (32.5%).
limits: Counts per category within 14 people; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: The costliest slip is repeating a failed fix. A code-side rule for the agent: after the same failing output twice, force a change of hypothesis (a G1 signal).

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri et al. (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development
finding: Developers proposed their own fixes: show several alternative solutions, log and categorise errors, ask clarifying questions when the same issue returns.
numbers: Proposals from interviews, not tested. They target fixation and belief confirmation.
limits: A wish list, no measured effect.
agent_relevance: Hints for the scaffold, but untested; do not add without a head-to-head test (G7).

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Bias cues in software dilemmas flip model answers that were correct on the neutral version. Every model and every one of 8 biases showed some sensitivity.
numbers: 16 seed tasks, 8 biases, answers checked against Prolog. Average sensitivity from 5.9% (anchoring) to 35.3% (hindsight). Median below 33%. Six systems from GPT, LLaMA and DeepSeek families.
limits: Short text dilemmas with two options, not code. Wording changes may trigger other biases. Proprietary models drift.
agent_relevance: Correct and robust are different things. Test the agent on paired neutral and cued prompts.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio (2025) Is General-Purpose AI Reasoning Sensitive to Data-Induced Cognitive Biases? (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Sensitivity grows with reasoning depth, so bigger or longer thinking does not remove it. Models can notice bias without resisting it.
numbers: Sensitivity rises with Prolog inference steps for 5 of 8 biases, up to 49%. Bias-awareness score 0.5 (GPT-4.1 Mini) to 0.8 (GPT-4o Mini), yet high sensitivity to hyperbolic discounting.
limits: The mitigations the authors list are proposals, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 and section 4b: awareness prompts are not the fix; a code-side cross-check is.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Prompt-based mitigations differ by model. Telling the model to be aware of bias helped little; counterfactual examples sometimes failed completely; having the model rewrite the prompt to remove the bias cue worked best.
numbers: 13,465 prompts, biases include framing, status quo, group attribution, anchoring, primacy. Self-help rewrite left 0% biased group-attribution prompts and 2.7% framing for GPT-4; Llama-2 7B left 1.4% framing and 6% status quo.
limits: Admissions decisions, not code. Anchoring self-help in Llama changed 40 to 52% of decisions, so it is unstable for small models.
agent_relevance: Cleaning the prompt beats telling the model to be careful. Rewriting by a strong model works; weak models do not.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Primacy: first-listed options are chosen more often. Awareness prompting reduced it slightly for Llama-2 7B and GPT-4.
numbers: Qualitative from figures; exact rates not extracted.
limits: Small effect, not shown for all models.
agent_relevance: Randomise or reorder candidate lists in code before any model picks (G5).

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld, Belinkov (2023) Instructed to Bias (COLM 2024)
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase cognitive-bias-like behaviour (decoy, certainty, belief bias) compared with the pretrained base.
numbers: Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 show higher bias than base counterparts. Pairs compared: T5 vs Flan-T5, Mistral vs Mistral-Instruct. Exact percentages not extracted.
limits: Some pairs (DaVinci vs DaVinci-002) differ by more than tuning. GPT-4 base not available.
agent_relevance: The chat-tuned model an agent uses may be more bias-prone than its base. A rival to the idea that tuning only helps.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (ICML)
finding: One irrelevant sentence in a math problem breaks the model, a slip like a human reading error. Remedies: sampling many times, an instruction to ignore irrelevant text, examples with distractors.
numbers: Of problems solved by greedy decoding, no more than 18% were solved for all types of irrelevant info. Under 30% of base problems consistently solved. Self-consistency with 20 samples: micro accuracy up over 11 points (35.5 points for zero-shot CoT); the correct answer is among 20 samples for 99.7% of problems.
limits: Math word problems (GSM-IC) on 2022 models. The ignore instruction did not lower accuracy on clean GSM8K.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4 and G11 style fixes: several short attempts with a code-side vote cut distraction errors. A specific ignore-irrelevant line helps, unlike a generic careful line.

source: Abdelsalam, Toneva, Apel (2025) How do Humans and LLMs Process Confusing Code?
finding: Code an LLM finds surprising (perplexity) matches where humans show a brain response to confusing code. Atoms of confusion raise model perplexity.
numbers: EEG plus eye-tracking data from 24 people, 72 Java snippets with clean twins. Spearman rho 0.47, p<0.001 for confusing snippets; rho 0.05, p=0.664 for clean ones. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B.
limits: Preprint, one model, short Java snippets. Perplexity is a proxy, not proof of confusion in reasoning.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side signal (token surprise) can flag spots where a slip is likely. Could feed the impasse detector, but untested for debugging.

source: Abdelsalam, Toneva, Apel (2025) How do Humans and LLMs Process Confusing Code?
finding: A data-driven detector based on perplexity peaks found most hand-labelled atoms and extra suspect regions.
numbers: Detected 64% of manually labelled atoms; 227 distinct regions flagged.
limits: Precision not established; extra regions not verified as real confusion.
agent_relevance: A candidate low-cost locator before running checks; needs a test against real defects.

source: Tambon et al. (2024) Bugs in Large Language Models Generated Code: An Empirical Study
finding: Model-written code has its own bug types, some rare in human code. The most common is misreading the task.
numbers: 333 bugs from CodeGen, PanGu-Coder, Codex; 10 patterns. Misinterpretation 20.77% of bugs. Survey of 34 practitioners: 80% often or always meet bugs in LLM code. Prompt-biased code and non-prompted consideration fall as the task gets more runnable.
limits: Old models; 8.9% survey return; patterns from open coding without inter-rater agreement.
agent_relevance: Human slip lists do not map one to one. Hallucinated objects and wrong attributes are rarely human slips; a static check (lint, run) catches these.

source: Fucci, Scanniello, Romano, Juristo (2018/2020) Need for Sleep: the Impact of a Night of Sleep Deprivation on Novice Developers' Performance (IEEE TSE)
finding: Moderator: one night without sleep roughly halves functional correctness of novice code, and syntax-fix editing rose.
numbers: Quasi-experiment, N=45 (23 sleep deprived, 22 normal). Correctness (share of asserts passed) about 50% lower, medium negative effect, CI -1.58 to -0.20. Syntax-fixing edits 54% higher.
limits: Not randomised (volunteers, 45 of 95). Activity (43% fewer actions) and test-first adherence: not significant after correction. Novices, small task, sleep not directly observed (a vigilance test was used).
agent_relevance: An agent has no fatigue; the nearest analogue is context length and load, untested here. Low relevance.

source: Fucci, Scanniello, Romano, Juristo (2018/2020) Need for Sleep: the Impact of a Night of Sleep Deprivation on Novice Developers' Performance (IEEE TSE)
finding: Authors rejected a repeated-measures design because of learning effects. Effects on engagement and process were not established.
numbers: Cleaned sleep-deprived set of 15 (8 doubtful participants removed) gave similar results. Engagement CI -1.31 to 0.04; process CI -1.18 to 0.15; both include zero.
limits: Single study; no replication seen in this session.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as settled. Time pressure and fatigue moderators are thinly supported for debugging.

source: Gopstein et al. (2017) Understanding misunderstandings in source code (ESEC/FSE)
finding: Original atoms of confusion study in C: 73 programmers shown code with and without atoms, plus a second check using IOCCC programs. Only the abstract reached me.
numbers: 73 programmers (from a search abstract). No effect sizes read.
limits: Not opened. The Java replication above cites this as the baseline.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the 2021 Java replication. Use the replication's numbers.
